answer: FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded): The data are consistent with the hypothesis that increased time preference (greater present-orientation/impatience) is associated with higher BMI. In the NLSY79 cohort, young adults who actively saved (put more money into savings in 1989 — the lowest time-preference group, measured 3 years BEFORE the 1992 outcome) had significantly lower BMI 1992 than every other group: ~0.40–0.47 BMI units lower (no-savings +0.47, took-out +0.40, no-change +0.40 vs put-in; all p≤0.01, fully adjusted incl. baseline BMI 1981) and lower odds of obesity at 1992 (OR 1.38–1.90 for non-savers/dis-savers vs savers). Raw means were monotone: put-in 25.43 < took-out 26.18 ≈ no-change 26.17 < no-savings 26.76, and raw obesity 13.9% vs 18.7–22.6%. The effect is modest in size (~0.08 SD ≈ 0.4–0.5 BMI units; ~3 lbs at median height) but statistically robust across the pre-registered contrasts (impatient-vs-patient, saver-vs-not) and across sensitivity checks (BMI 1989, ΔBMI 1981→1992, obesity), and directionally consistent in 7 of 8 proxy variants (savings order, savings categories, saver-vs-not, wealth-for-income, sentenced, composite all positive; only the rare jail-any indicator — 2.4% prevalence, p=0.35 — flipped sign). Because this is observational, I state the finding as an association consistent with the causal question and CANNOT assert that time preference causally "leads to" higher BMI; residual confounding (health motivation, genetics, local food environment) and reverse causality remain possible, and the fully-adjusted sample (5,317 of 12,686; 58.1% lost) limits generalizability. Answer to the question: Yes — higher time preference is associated with significantly higher BMI, in a direction consistent with a causal role, but not proven causally by these data.

payload.hypothesis: Higher time preference (present-orientation/impatience) is associated with significantly higher BMI in early adulthood: 1989 savers (put more money into savings, the lowest time-preference group) had BMI in 1992 about 0.4–0.5 units lower (≈0.08 SD) and 38–90% lower odds of obesity than dis-savers/non-savers, after adjustment for SES, education, race/ethnicity, sex, age, family background, cognitive ability and baseline BMI. The pattern is consistent with a causal role of time preference but is an observational association, not proof of causation.
payload.workflow: 1) Unit forensics: heights 1981 decoded from feet+inches; weights confirmed as pounds though codebook says kg (validated by BMI plausibility). 2) BMI outcomes built for 1981/1989/1992 (703*lbs/in^2), implausible values excluded. 3) Time-preference proxies: primary = 1989 savings direction (put_in/took_out/no_change/no_savings) with impatient-vs-patient and saver-vs-not contrasts; secondary = wealth-for-income residual, jailed/incarceration indicators; composite as robustness. 4) OLS/GLM models: bivariate and fully-adjusted (sex, race, age89, education, log income89, parental education, family size, ASVAB, sampling stratum, baseline BMI81); outcomes BMI 1992 (primary), BMI 1989, ΔBMI 1981-92, obesity>=30 (secondary). 5) Missingness/attrition reported at each sample; analytic vs full-file comparisons on observables. 6) Sign-consistency across 8 proxy variants assessed before wording.
